Following this observation, we propose teaching the model to reason more robustly by folding the provided contextual knowledge into the model's parameters before presenting it with a question. Our method, RECKONING, is a bi-level learning algorithm that teaches language models to reason by updating their parametric knowledge through back-propagation, allowing them to then answer questions using the updated parameters. During training, the inner loop rapidly adapts a copy of the model weights to encode contextual knowledge into its parameters. In the outer loop, the model learns to use the updated weights to reproduce and answer reasoning questions about the memorized knowledge. Our experiments on two multi-hop reasoning datasets show that RECKONING's performance improves over the in-context reasoning baseline (by up to 4.5%). We also find that compared to in-context reasoning, RECKONING generalizes better to longer reasoning chains unseen during training, is more robust to distractors in the context, and is more computationally efficient when multiple questions are asked about the same knowledge.

papers.title: Small Vectors, Big Effects: A Mechanistic Study of RL-Induced Reasoning via Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How does reasoning training reshape LLMs' internal computations, and what are the mechanisms of trainable steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Lightweight steering vectors trained with an RL objective explain a large portion of full fine-tuning performance increase while preserving interpretability, and their mechanisms (e.g., token substitution at the last layer, MLP-mediated effects at the penultimate layer) are elucidated.
papers.conclusion: Steering vectors provide a compact and informative probe of reasoning-trained models, offering concrete insight into how RL-induced changes manifest in token preferences and internal circuitry.
papers.key_findings:
The last-layer steering vector acts like a token-substitution bias concentrated on the first generated token, boosting tokens such as 'To' and 'Step'.
The penultimate-layer vector leaves attention patterns largely intact and operates through the MLP and unembedding, up-weighting process words and structure symbols.
Steering vectors transfer to other models from the same family, suggesting underlying directions are preserved under fine-tuning.
Early-layer steering does not express later-layer steering directions; induced shifts diffuse and become nearly orthogonal to later-layer vectors.
Single-layer steering vectors isolate layer-specific effects and provide an upper bound on linear intervention performance at that layer.
papers.limitation: The effects are consistently stronger and cleaner in Qwen than in Llama, suggesting model-specific implementations of similar high-level behaviors.
future_direction: Systematic comparisons across architectures and training recipes to explain differences in steering vector effects.
Pin down the precise mechanisms of mid-layer steering vectors, which are harder to localize to a single submodule.
papers.abstract: The mechanisms by which reasoning training reshapes LLMs' internal computations remain unclear. We study lightweight steering vectors inserted into the base model's residual stream and trained with a reinforcement-learning objective. These vectors explain a large portion of full fine-tuning performance increase while preserving the interpretability of small, additive interventions. We find that (i) the last-layer steering vector acts like a token-substitution bias concentrated on the first generated token, consistently boosting tokens such as "To" and "Step"; (ii) the penultimate-layer vector leaves attention patterns largely intact and instead operates through the MLP and unembedding, preferentially up-weighting process words and structure symbols; and (iii) the steering vectors transfer to other models from the same family. Taken together, these results deepen understanding of how trained steering vectors shape computation and should inform future work in activation engineering and the study of reasoning models.

papers.title: Scaling Reasoning Hop Exposes Weaknesses: Demystifying and Improving Hop Generalization in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: The paper investigates where errors occur in reasoning hop generalization (RQ1) and why these errors arise (RQ2), focusing on the internal mechanisms of LLMs.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes Test-time Correction of Reasoning (TCR), a lightweight intervention method that dynamically identifies and deactivates erroneous processing heads to improve reasoning hop generalization, based on mechanistic insights into internal competition mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that TCR effectively improves reasoning hop generalization by dynamically deactivating erroneous processing heads, demonstrating the potential of test-time interventions based on mechanistic insights.
papers.key_findings:
Errors in reasoning hop generalization are dominated by token-level erroneous predictions of a few specific error types, enabling focused diagnosis.
These token-level errors stem from an internal competition mechanism: correct trajectories coexist with erroneous ones but are actively suppressed by erroneous processing heads; knocking out such heads can restore correct predictions.
The proposed TCR method, which automatically and dynamically deactivates erroneous processing heads, consistently improves reasoning hop generalization across tasks and models.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has become the standard paradigm for enabling Large Language Models (LLMs) to solve complex problems. However, recent studies reveal a sharp performance drop in reasoning hop generalization scenarios, where the required number of reasoning steps exceeds training distributions while the underlying algorithm remains unchanged. The internal mechanisms driving this failure remain poorly understood. In this work, we conduct a systematic study on tasks from multiple domains, and find that errors concentrate at token positions of a few critical error types, rather than being uniformly distributed. Closer inspection reveals that these token-level erroneous predictions stem from internal competition mechanisms: certain attention heads, termed erroneous processing heads (ep heads), tip the balance by amplifying incorrect reasoning trajectories while suppressing correct ones. Notably, removing individual ep heads during inference can often restore the correct predictions. Motivated by these insights, we propose test-time correction of reasoning, a lightweight intervention method that dynamically identifies and deactivates ep heads in the reasoning process. Extensive experiments across different tasks and LLMs show that it consistently improves reasoning hop generalization, highlighting both its effectiveness and potential.

papers.title: From Yes-Men to Truth-Tellers: Addressing Sycophancy in Large Language Models with Pinpoint Tuning
papers.research_question: How can we address sycophancy in Large Language Models by pinpointing and tuning only the components responsible for this behavior, without degrading their general capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes supervised pinpoint tuning (SPT), a method that identifies a sparse set of attention heads responsible for sycophancy using path patching and then fine-tunes only those heads, effectively mitigating sycophancy while preserving the model's general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Pinpoint tuning is an effective and efficient method to address sycophancy in LLMs by targeting specific internal components, advancing both the understanding and intervention of model behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Only a small percentage (~4%) of attention heads significantly influence sycophantic behavior, as identified by path patching.
Pinpoint tuning these heads effectively reduces sycophancy, outperforming supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on sycophancy metrics.
Pinpoint tuning preserves general capabilities (e.g., reasoning, math, code) unlike SFT, which often degrades them.
The method generalizes beyond the training data, as shown on additional sycophancy evaluation datasets.
The identified sycophancy-related heads attend more to tokens that challenge the model compared to other heads.
papers.limitation:
Path patching treats each MLP and attention head as individual nodes, but future work could consider neurons or groups of neurons as atomic units for more refined analysis.
The evaluation is based on a specific definition of sycophancy (from Sharma et al. 2023), and it is unclear whether the results generalize to other formats of sycophancy.
The verification of pinpoint tuning is mainly conducted on sycophancy; its effectiveness for other abilities requires further investigation.
future_direction: Treating neurons or groups of neurons as atomic units for analysis instead of heads and MLPs.
Investigating generalization to other formats and definitions of sycophancy.
Integrating pinpoint tuning with other interpretability tools like information flow, representation engineering, and sparse auto-encoders.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) tend to prioritize adherence to user prompts over providing veracious responses, leading to the sycophancy issue. When challenged by users, LLMs tend to admit mistakes and provide inaccurate responses even if they initially provided the correct answer. Recent works propose to employ supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to mitigate the sycophancy issue, while it typically leads to the degeneration of LLMs' general capability. To address the challenge, we propose a novel supervised pinpoint tuning (SPT), where the region-of-interest modules are tuned for a given objective. Specifically, SPT first reveals and verifies a small percentage (<5%) of the basic modules, which significantly affect a particular behavior of LLMs. i.e., sycophancy. Subsequently, SPT merely fine-tunes these identified modules while freezing the rest. To verify the effectiveness of the proposed SPT, we conduct comprehensive experiments, demonstrating that SPT significantly mitigates the sycophancy issue of LLMs (even better than SFT). Moreover, SPT introduces limited or even no side effects on the general capability of LLMs. Our results shed light on how to precisely, effectively, and efficiently explain and improve the targeted ability of LLMs. Code and data are available at https://github.com/yellowtownhz/sycophancy-interpretability.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Large-Scale Counting in LLMs through a System-2 Strategy
papers.research_question: How can a test-time strategy inspired by System-2 cognitive processes overcome the architectural limitations of LLMs in large-scale counting tasks, and what are the underlying mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a simple test-time strategy that decomposes large counting tasks into smaller sub-problems, enabling LLMs to surpass their architectural limitations and achieve high accuracy, and provides a mechanistic interpretation of how this System-2-like strategy functions within the models.
papers.conclusion: The proposed System-2 test-time strategy effectively overcomes the architectural limitations of LLMs in large-scale counting by decomposing the task, and mechanistic analysis reveals how count information is stored, transferred, and aggregated within the model.
papers.key_findings:
A System-2 strategy combining structured input (partitioning with a separator) and intermediate reasoning steps (Chain-of-Thought) enables LLMs to accurately count large numbers of items, overcoming the performance degradation seen in standard (System-1) counting.
Attention analysis shows that during intermediate reasoning, the model attends strongly to the final item/separator of each partition in middle-to-late layers (e.g., layers 19-23), and during final answer generation, it attends to the intermediate count tokens.
Causal mediation analysis (activation patching) identifies that count information is stored in the final item representations of each partition, transferred via specific attention heads, and aggregated to produce the final total.
The model's internal counting mechanism (System-1) is capacity-limited and degrades for counts beyond approximately 30 items due to transformer depth constraints, explaining the failure on large-scale counting.
Neither structured input alone nor Chain-of-Thought reasoning alone is sufficient for accurate large-scale counting; their combination is necessary.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on a narrow counting task with limited object diversity, using simple repeated nouns in synthetic contexts.
The approach depends on structured prompts and assumes prior knowledge of the model's reliable counting range, which may limit generalization.
The effects of tokenization and number representation are not isolated and may independently influence the results.
future_direction: Explore further applications of this strategy to complex reasoning tasks in language and beyond.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs), despite strong performance on complex mathematical problems, exhibit systematic limitations in counting tasks. This issue arises from architectural limits of transformers, where counting is performed across layers, leading to degraded precision for larger counting problems due to depth constraints. To address this limitation, we propose a simple test-time strategy inspired by System-2 cognitive processes that decomposes large counting tasks into smaller, independent sub-problems that the model can reliably solve. We evaluate this approach using observational and causal mediation analyses to understand the underlying mechanism of this System-2-like strategy. Our mechanistic analysis identifies key components: latent counts are computed and stored in the final item representations of each part, transferred to intermediate steps via dedicated attention heads, and aggregated in the final stage to produce the total count. Experimental results demonstrate that this strategy enables LLMs to surpass architectural limitations and achieve high accuracy on large-scale counting tasks. This work provides mechanistic insight into System-2 counting in LLMs and presents a generalizable approach for improving and understanding their reasoning behavior.

papers.title: Associative memory inspires improvements for in-context learning using a novel attention residual stream architecture
papers.research_question: How can insights from associative memory models be used to improve in-context learning (ICL) in Transformer-based language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a novel residual attention stream architecture, inspired by associative memory, that allows information to flow directly between attention heads, leading to faster and improved in-context learning in Transformers.
papers.conclusion: The residual attention stream architecture, inspired by associative memory models, improves in-context learning in Transformers and shows promising scalability to larger language models.
papers.key_findings:
A one-layer associative memory model (AMICL) can perform in-context learning on a classification task.
Adding a residual stream for attention values (and to a lesser extent, queries) in a two-layer Transformer speeds up the emergence of ICL during training compared to a classic Transformer.
Naively applying the residual value stream architecture to small language models (8M and 1B parameters) trained on Tiny Stories indicates performance improvements scale to larger models and more naturalistic data.
future_direction: Testing the residual attention stream architecture on larger models and more complex tasks.
Exploring the interpretability of the residual stream for understanding model mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate an impressive ability to utilise information within the context of their input sequences to appropriately respond to data unseen by the LLM during its training procedure. This ability is known as in-context learning (ICL). Humans and non-human animals demonstrate similar abilities, however their neural architectures differ substantially from LLMs. Despite this, a critical component within LLMs, the attention mechanism, resembles modern associative memory models, widely used in and influenced by the computational neuroscience community to model biological memory systems. Using this connection, we introduce an associative memory model capable of performing ICL. We use this as inspiration for a novel residual stream architecture which allows information to directly flow between attention heads. We test this architecture during training within a two-layer Transformer and show its ICL abilities manifest more quickly than without this modification. We then apply our architecture in small language models with 8 million and 1 billion parameters, focusing on attention head values, with results also indicating improved performance at these larger and more naturalistic scales.

papers.title: Scaling Laws and Interpretability of Learning from Repeated Data
papers.research_question: What are the effects of repeated data on language model training, and how does it mechanistically affect model components like induction heads?
papers.core_contribution: Repeated data causes a double-descent phenomenon in language models, leading to severe performance degradation that is mechanistically linked to disproportionate damage to induction heads and copying mechanisms, shifting the model from generalization to memorization.
papers.conclusion: Small fractions of repeated data, if repeated at a specific frequency, can cause surprisingly severe performance degradation in language models, and this degradation is associated with disproportionate damage to internal mechanisms like induction heads that support generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Repeated data induces a strong double-descent phenomenon, with a predictable range of repetition frequency causing severe performance degradation.
A small fraction of repeated data (e.g., 0.1% repeated 100 times) can degrade an 800M parameter model's performance to that of a 400M parameter model.
Repeated data disproportionately damages copying ability and induction heads, which are internal structures associated with generalization.
The damage to induction heads provides a mechanistic explanation for the shift from generalization to memorization.
The double-descent phenomenon and associated performance degradation are also observed when training on Python code data.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have been trained on vast datasets, but also often on repeated data, either intentionally for the purpose of upweighting higher quality data, or unintentionally because data deduplication is not perfect and the model is exposed to repeated data at the sentence, paragraph, or document level. Some works have reported substantial negative performance effects of this repeated data. In this paper we attempt to study repeated data systematically and to understand its effects mechanistically. To do this, we train a family of models where most of the data is unique but a small fraction of it is repeated many times. We find a strong double descent phenomenon, in which repeated data can lead test loss to increase midway through training. A predictable range of repetition frequency leads to surprisingly severe degradation in performance. For instance, performance of an 800M parameter model can be degraded to that of a 2x smaller model (400M params) by repeating 0.1% of the data 100 times, despite the other 90% of the training tokens remaining unique. We suspect there is a range in the middle where the data can be memorized and doing so consumes a large fraction of the model's capacity, and this may be where the peak of degradation occurs. Finally, we connect these observations to recent mechanistic interpretability work - attempting to reverse engineer the detailed computations performed by the model - by showing that data repetition disproportionately damages copying and internal structures associated with generalization, such as induction heads, providing a possible mechanism for the shift from generalization to memorization. Taken together, these results provide a hypothesis for why repeating a relatively small fraction of data in large language models could lead to disproportionately large harms to performance.

papers.title: ReJump: A Tree-Jump Representation for Analyzing and Improving LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: How can we represent an LLM’s reasoning trace to facilitate a comprehensive analysis and comparison of its internal behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ReJump, a tree-jump representation for LLM reasoning traces, enabling comprehensive analysis and comparison of reasoning behaviors, and demonstrates its utility for improving reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: ReJump provides a comprehensive framework for analyzing and comparing LLM reasoning behaviors, and can be leveraged to improve reasoning accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Models with similar final accuracy can exhibit distinct reasoning behaviors.
Different tasks favor different reasoning styles (e.g., varying balance between exploration and exploitation).
LRMs exhibit more deliberate reasoning behaviors (e.g., exploration and verification) compared to CoT-prompted LLMs.
Distilled models inherit reasoning behaviors from their teachers.
ReJump can improve reasoning quality at test time through strategies such as ReJump-guided Best-of-N selection and prompt selection.
papers.limitation: Tree and jump similarity metrics only capture logical structure and action-transition distributions, overlooking semantic content and temporal patterns.
future_direction: Incorporating semantic information and temporal dynamics into the ReJump representation and metrics.
papers.abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) are Large Language Models (LLMs) explicitly trained to generate long-form Chain-of-Thoughts (CoTs), achieving impressive success on challenging tasks like math and programming. However, their underlying reasoning "algorithms" remain poorly understood. To investigate this, we propose ReJump, which represents a reasoning trace as a visitation order over nodes in a tree of intermediate problem-solving steps. Transitions between nodes, which we term jumps, include adjacent moves that capture behaviors such as calculation, and non-adjacent moves that capture behaviors such as backtracking and verification. ReJump enables analyzing LLM reasoning with diverse metrics that quantify exploration, exploitation, overthinking, forgetting, and verification. Using our proposed LLM agent to extract reasoning traces into ReJump format, we evaluate state-of-the-art LRMs on two tasks and find that models with similar accuracy can exhibit distinct reasoning behaviors, while different tasks favor different reasoning styles (e.g., varying balance between exploration and exploitation). To further understand how learning strategies shape reasoning, we use ReJump to compare distilled LRMs with their teachers, CoT-prompted LLMs with LRMs, and to examine how the number of reasoning examples and reinforcement learning affect reasoning behavior. Finally, we show that ReJump can improve reasoning quality at test time through strategies such as ReJump-guided Best-of-N selection and prompt selection. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/UW-Madison-Lee-Lab/ReJump.

papers.title: Do Latent-CoT Models Think Step-by-Step? A Mechanistic Study on Sequential Reasoning Tasks
papers.research_question: Does latent chain-of-thought (specifically CODI) implement genuine step-by-step reasoning on sequential tasks, or does it rely on shortcuts and late-stage fusion?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that latent CoT (CODI) implements step-by-step reasoning only for short hops (2-3) and shifts to a partial, late-bottleneck strategy for longer tasks, with performance and mechanism depending on the compressibility of the task (composite vs prime moduli).
papers.conclusion: With composite moduli, CODI is step-by-step on 2–3 hops but shifts to a late-intermediate partial rollout on longer horizons; with prime moduli, it largely fails to learn and shows neither signature. The split is explained by compressibility: composite moduli induce many-to-one contractions that bias the label toward late updates, making the computation compressible, while prime moduli lack this structure.
papers.key_findings:
For 2-3 hop polynomial tasks, CODI forms bridge states in the latent channel and fuses them with the final input at the answer readout.
For longer hop tasks (n>=4), CODI collapses to a partial latent rollout, representing only the last one or two intermediate states.
There is a prime-composite split: under composite moduli, CODI succeeds with a late-bottleneck strategy; under prime moduli, performance drops and step-by-step reasoning fails.
The final input is routed directly to the answer readout via a copy-like pathway, separate from the latent channel.
Teacher-guided compression drives the partial-reasoning strategy under composite moduli.
papers.limitation: CODI struggles with incompressible sequential tasks (e.g., prime moduli) due to fixed latent-compute budget.
future_direction: Test whether the compressibility dependence (including the prime–composite split) persists across latent-CoT objectives and architectures.
Develop adaptive mechanisms that allocate latent compute to match task demands.
Extend the mechanistic toolbox to more sequential and naturalistic datasets.
papers.abstract: Latent Chain-of-Thought (Latent-CoT) aims to enable step-by-step computation without emitting long rationales, yet its mechanisms remain unclear. We study CODI, a continuous-thought teacher-student distillation model, on strictly sequential polynomial-iteration tasks. Using logit-lens decoding, linear probes, attention analysis, and activation patching, we localize intermediate-state representations and trace their routing to the final readout. On two- and three-hop tasks, CODI forms the full set of bridge states that become decodable across latent-thought positions, while the final input follows a separate near-direct route; predictions arise via late fusion at the end-of-thought boundary. For longer hop lengths, CODI does not reliably execute a full latent rollout, instead exhibiting a partial latent reasoning path that concentrates on late intermediates and fuses them with the last input at the answer readout position. Ablations show that this partial pathway can collapse under regime shifts, including harder optimization. Overall, we delineate when CODI-style latent-CoT yields faithful iterative computation versus compressed or shortcut strategies, and highlight challenges in designing robust latent-CoT objectives for sequential reasoning.

papers.title: Disentangling Memory and Reasoning Ability in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we disentangle memory recall and reasoning steps in large language models to improve performance and interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a novel LLM inference paradigm that disentangles memory recall and reasoning steps using special tokens, enhancing both accuracy and interpretability in complex QA tasks.
papers.conclusion: The proposed decomposition of memory and reasoning steps in LLMs leads to improved performance and greater interpretability, enabling better error analysis and model refinement.
papers.key_findings:
The method improves LLM performance on StrategyQA, CommonsenseQA, and TruthfulQA benchmarks, outperforming baselines like CoT and planning tokens.
On TruthfulQA, the enhanced LLaMA-3.1-8B model achieves 86.6% accuracy, surpassing GPT-4o with CoT prompting.
Error analysis reveals that most errors originate from reasoning steps rather than memory recall, highlighting reasoning as the primary challenge.
The decomposition enhances interpretability by allowing clear separation of memory and reasoning steps in the inference process.
Attention analysis shows that special tokens receive higher attention weights, indicating their role in guiding knowledge and reasoning content generation.
papers.limitation:
Dependency on training data quality for memory recall
Token utilization complexity due to special tokens
Performance may struggle with highly complex reasoning tasks
Computation overhead from decomposing steps
future_direction: Dynamic memory updating to incorporate new information without retraining.
Adaptive reasoning steps based on task complexity.
Interpretable error analysis tools for tracing failures to memory or reasoning steps.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance in handling complex tasks requiring both extensive knowledge and reasoning abilities. However, the existing LLM inference pipeline operates as an opaque process without explicit separation between knowledge retrieval and reasoning steps, making the model's decision-making process unclear and disorganized. This ambiguity can lead to issues such as hallucinations and knowledge forgetting, which significantly impact the reliability of LLMs in high-stakes domains. In this paper, we propose a new inference paradigm that decomposes the complex inference process into two distinct and clear actions: (1) memory recall: which retrieves relevant knowledge, and (2) reasoning: which performs logical steps based on the recalled knowledge. To facilitate this decomposition, we introduce two special tokens memory and reason, guiding the model to distinguish between steps that require knowledge retrieval and those that involve reasoning. Our experiment results show that this decomposition not only improves model performance but also enhances the interpretability of the inference process, enabling users to identify sources of error and refine model responses effectively. The code is available at https://github.com/MingyuJ666/Disentangling-Memory-and-Reasoning.

papers.title: InversionView: A General-Purpose Method for Reading Information from Neural Activations
papers.research_question: How can we decipher the information encoded in neural activations? The paper proposes InversionView, a method to sample from the preimage of an activation to uncover the information content.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces InversionView, a method that samples from the preimage of an activation via a conditional decoder to uncover the information encoded in neural activations and understand model algorithms.
papers.conclusion: InversionView is a general-purpose method that effectively deciphers information in neural activations, enabling better understanding of model algorithms and simplifying interpretability workflows.
papers.key_findings:
InversionView can reveal both basic and complex information in activations, such as token counts and relative positions.
InversionView simplifies interpretability workflows, agreeing with prior circuit findings in GPT-2 small.
InversionView enabled the first fully verified circuit for a 3-digit addition model.
InversionView scales to larger models like GPT-2 for factual recall.
papers.limitation:
Training a decoder requires a dataset of activations and can be computationally expensive.
The decoder may not perfectly capture the preimage, leading to potential biases in the generated samples.
The method is currently limited to discrete sequences (text).
future_direction: Extend InversionView to continuous domains.
Improve decoder efficiency.
Automate interpretation using LLMs.
papers.abstract: The inner workings of neural networks can be better understood if we can fully decipher the information encoded in neural activations. In this paper, we argue that this information is embodied by the subset of inputs that give rise to similar activations. We propose InversionView, which allows us to practically inspect this subset by sampling from a trained decoder model conditioned on activations. This helps uncover the information content of activation vectors, and facilitates understanding of the algorithms implemented by transformer models. We present four case studies where we investigate models ranging from small transformers to GPT-2. In these studies, we show that InversionView can reveal clear information contained in activations, including basic information about tokens appearing in the context, as well as more complex information, such as the count of certain tokens, their relative positions, and abstract knowledge about the subject. We also provide causally verified circuits to confirm the decoded information.

papers.title: MLPs Learn In-Context on Regression and Classification Tasks
papers.research_question: Can multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) learn in-context, and how does their performance compare to Transformers on synthetic in-context learning and relational reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: MLPs can learn in-context on synthetic regression and classification tasks comparably to Transformers under the same compute budget, and outperform Transformers on classical relational reasoning tasks, challenging prior assumptions about their capabilities.
papers.conclusion: MLPs are capable of in-context learning and relational reasoning, challenging prior arguments against their ability, and encouraging further study of MLP architectures in more complex settings to understand the comparative advantage of attention-based schemes.
papers.key_findings:
MLPs can learn in-context on regression and classification tasks.
MLPs perform comparably to Transformers on ICL tasks under the same compute budget.
MLPs outperform Transformers on relational reasoning tasks (match-to-sample, sphere oddball, line oddball).
MLPs exhibit a transition from in-weight learning to in-context learning as data diversity increases, similar to Transformers.
Vanilla MLPs struggle with long context lengths in ICL regression, but MLP-Mixers do not.
papers.limitation: It remains unclear how MLPs perform against Transformers at scale on real-world tasks, and where a performance gap may originate.
future_direction: Further exploration of MLP architectures in more complex settings to better understand the potential comparative advantage of attention-based schemes.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL), the remarkable ability to solve a task from only input exemplars, is often assumed to be a unique hallmark of Transformer models. By examining commonly employed synthetic ICL tasks, we demonstrate that multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) can also learn in-context. Moreover, MLPs, and the closely related MLP-Mixer models, learn in-context comparably with Transformers under the same compute budget in this setting. We further show that MLPs outperform Transformers on a series of classical tasks from psychology designed to test relational reasoning, which are closely related to in-context classification. These results underscore a need for studying in-context learning beyond attention-based architectures, while also challenging prior arguments against MLPs' ability to solve relational tasks. Altogether, our results highlight the unexpected competence of MLPs in a synthetic setting, and support the growing interest in all-MLP alternatives to Transformer architectures. It remains unclear how MLPs perform against Transformers at scale on real-world tasks, and where a performance gap may originate. We encourage further exploration of these architectures in more complex settings to better understand the potential comparative advantage of attention-based schemes.

papers.title: Unveiling Reasoning Thresholds in Language Models: Scaling, Fine-Tuning, and Interpretability through Attention Maps
papers.research_question: What is the critical parameter threshold for reasoning abilities in decoder-only transformer-based language models, and how can fine-tuning and attention map analysis improve understanding of these capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a critical parameter threshold (~1.6B) for reasoning abilities in language models, shows fine-tuning improves sub-threshold models, and uses attention maps to interpret reasoning processes.
papers.conclusion: The study identifies a critical parameter threshold for reasoning, demonstrates fine-tuning efficacy for sub-threshold models, and uses attention maps for interpretability, advancing understanding of reasoning in decoder-only transformer-based language models.
papers.key_findings:
Models above ~1.6 billion parameters show significant improvement in reasoning performance on tasks like commonsense QA and deductive reasoning.
Fine-tuning sub-threshold models with task-specific exemplars substantially improves performance on simpler deductive rules (e.g., implication elimination, conjunction introduction).
Attention map analysis reveals that models generating correct chain-of-thought exhibit higher token-level attention scores on subsequent correct tokens and correct parts of speech.
Parameter gaps exist for specific deductive rules: disjunction elimination (~1.1B) and proof by contradiction (~1.6B).
Smaller models (below threshold) struggle with structured answer formatting, resulting in high rates of unparseable responses.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the in-context learning capabilities of various decoder-only transformer-based language models with different model sizes and training data, including GPT2, SmolLM2, OpenELM, TinyLlama, Stable LM, and Gemma 2. We identify a critical parameter threshold (~1.6 billion), beyond which reasoning performance improves significantly in tasks such as commonsense reasoning in multiple-choice question answering and deductive reasoning. Specifically, models above this threshold achieve better success rates in chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting for deductive reasoning tasks, especially those requiring longer reasoning chains, such as proof by contradiction and disjunction elimination. To address limitations in sub-threshold models, we demonstrate that fine-tuning with task-specific exemplars substantially enhances reasoning performance, enabling accurate CoT generation even without additional exemplars in the prompt for tasks with shorter reasoning chains. Finally, our analysis of attention maps reveals that models capable of generating correct CoTs exhibit higher token-level attention scores on subsequent correct tokens and the correct parts of speech, providing interpretability insights into reasoning processes. These findings collectively advance understanding of reasoning capabilities in decoder-only transformer-based models. The code is available at: https://github.com/AnnonymousForPapers/CoT_Reasoning_Test.

papers.title: CircuitSeer: Mining High-Quality Data by Probing Mathematical Reasoning Circuits in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we select high-quality reasoning data for fine-tuning LLMs by leveraging the model's internal mechanisms, specifically sparse, specialized attention circuits, instead of relying on external heuristics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CircuitSeer, a data selection method that quantifies reasoning complexity by measuring the influence of training samples on sparse, specialized attention head circuits identified within a reference LLM, enabling efficient fine-tuning with small, high-quality subsets.
papers.conclusion: CircuitSeer provides an interpretable, model-internal signal for reasoning data quality, enabling efficient and effective data selection for fine-tuning LLMs, and demonstrates that internal reasoning circuits encode measurable structures of problem difficulty.
papers.key_findings:
A sparse, specialized subset of attention heads forms core reasoning circuits that are consistently activated during complex mathematical reasoning tasks.
Fine-tuning on just 10% of data selected by CircuitSeer can outperform training on the full dataset, achieving a 1.4-point gain in average Pass@1 on Qwen2.5-Math-7B.
Scoring based on input problem statements (rather than output reasoning traces) more effectively captures reasoning complexity.
Soft sampling based on CircuitSeer scores yields better performance and diversity than deterministic top-k selection.
The identified reasoning heads provide a clearer signal for data selection than using all heads or a random subset.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive reasoning capabilities, but scaling their performance often relies on massive reasoning datasets that are computationally expensive to train on. Existing data selection methods aim to curate smaller, high-quality subsets but often rely on costly external models or opaque heuristics. In this work, we shift the focus from external heuristics to the model's internal mechanisms. We find that complex reasoning tasks consistently activate a sparse, specialized subset of attention heads, forming core reasoning circuits. Building on this insight, we propose CircuitSeer, a novel data selection method that quantifies the reasoning complexity of data by measuring its influence on these crucial circuits. Extensive experiments on 4 models and 9 datasets demonstrate CircuitSeer's superiority. Notably, fine-tuning Qwen2.5-Math-7B on just 10% of data selected by our method achieves a 1.4-point gain in average Pass@1 over training on the full dataset, highlighting its efficiency and effectiveness.

papers.title: Mechanistic Indicators of Understanding in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) possess genuine understanding, and if so, what forms does it take? The paper investigates this by synthesizing findings from mechanistic interpretability within a philosophical framework.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a tiered framework (conceptual, state-of-the-world, principled understanding) for assessing understanding in LLMs and synthesizes mechanistic interpretability evidence to argue that LLMs can develop internal organizations that underwrite understanding-like unification, though these mechanisms diverge from human cognition.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability reveals internal organizations in LLMs that can underwrite understanding-like unification across conceptual, factual, and principled tiers, but these mechanisms diverge from human cognition in their parallel exploitation of heterogeneous, task-specific pathways.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs develop internal 'features' (e.g., a 'Golden Gate Bridge' feature in Claude 3 Sonnet) that act as conceptual unifiers, connecting diverse manifestations of entities or properties.
The linear representation hypothesis is supported, with features encoded as directions in latent space, and superposition allows for efficient representation of many features.
Models like Othello-GPT develop internal 'world models' (e.g., of the board state) that are causally involved in task performance, as shown via probing and intervention techniques.
The phenomenon of 'grokking' demonstrates a shift from memorization to discovering compact, generalizable circuits (e.g., for modular arithmetic), indicative of principled understanding.
Higher-tier understanding mechanisms coexist with lower-tier heuristics (e.g., memorization, n-gram statistics) within LLMs, impacting their epistemic trustworthiness.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often portrayed as merely imitating linguistic patterns without genuine understanding. We argue that recent findings in mechanistic interpretability (MI), the emerging field probing the inner workings of LLMs, render this picture increasingly untenable--but only once those findings are integrated within a theoretical account of understanding. We propose a tiered framework for thinking about understanding in LLMs and use it to synthesize the most relevant findings to date. The framework distinguishes three hierarchical varieties of understanding, each tied to a corresponding level of computational organization: conceptual understanding emerges when a model forms "features" as directions in latent space, learning connections between diverse manifestations of a single entity or property; state-of-the-world understanding emerges when a model learns contingent factual connections between features and dynamically tracks changes in the world; principled understanding emerges when a model ceases to rely on memorized facts and discovers a compact "circuit" connecting these facts. Across these tiers, MI uncovers internal organizations that can underwrite understanding-like unification. However, these also diverge from human cognition in their parallel exploitation of heterogeneous mechanisms. Fusing philosophical theory with mechanistic evidence thus allows us to transcend binary debates over whether AI understands, paving the way for a comparative, mechanistically grounded epistemology that explores how AI understanding aligns with--and diverges from--our own.

papers.title: Beyond Chains of Thought: Benchmarking Latent-Space Reasoning Abilities in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we quantify the internal reasoning abilities (reasoning leaps) of large language models, and to what extent do they engage in complex latent-space computations without explicit token generation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a benchmark to quantify latent-space reasoning leaps in LLMs, demonstrating that LLMs can perform internal reasoning and that performance varies across models and reasoning domains.
papers.conclusion: LLMs can perform latent-space reasoning, and larger dense models may have greater potential for internal reasoning, which has implications for safety and the need to monitor opaque internal computations.
papers.key_findings:
GPT-4.5 achieves the highest accuracy (74.7%) on the benchmark, outperforming other models like Grok-2 and Llama 3.1 405B.
Smaller models generally perform worse than larger models, but there are exceptions (e.g., Llama 3.1 70B and 405B perform similarly).
Models with MoE architectures (e.g., Llama 4 Maverick, DeepSeek-V3) underperform compared to dense models of similar total parameter count.
Performance varies across reasoning domains, with social, spatial, and temporal reasoning being more challenging than arithmetic, causal, logical, moral, and linguistic reasoning.
Control experiments suggest that models are not merely exploiting heuristics in the main benchmark, but are actually reasoning internally.
papers.limitation:
Models may exploit heuristics rather than engage in genuine reasoning, which is a limitation of the benchmark.
The benchmark cannot reliably determine when models shift from reasoning to heuristic-based strategies.
future_direction: Investigate the conditions under which LLMs rely on heuristics versus genuine internal reasoning.
Develop methods to better monitor latent-space reasoning to ensure the safe deployment of advanced LLMs.
Study the correlation between model size (and architecture) and latent-space reasoning abilities.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can perform reasoning computations both internally within their latent space and externally by generating explicit token sequences like chains of thought. Significant progress in enhancing reasoning abilities has been made by scaling test-time compute. However, understanding and quantifying model-internal reasoning abilities - the inferential "leaps" models make between individual token predictions - remains crucial. This study introduces a benchmark (n = 4,000 items) designed to quantify model-internal reasoning in different domains. We achieve this by having LLMs indicate the correct solution to reasoning problems not through descriptive text, but by selecting a specific language of their initial response token that is different from English, the benchmark language. This not only requires models to reason beyond their context window, but also to overrise their default tendency to respond in the same language as the prompt, thereby posing an additional cognitive strain. We evaluate a set of 18 LLMs, showing significant performance variations, with GPT-4.5 achieving the highest accuracy (74.7%), outperforming models like Grok-2 (67.2%), and Llama 3.1 405B (65.6%). Control experiments and difficulty scaling analyses suggest that while LLMs engage in internal reasoning, we cannot rule out heuristic exploitations under certain conditions, marking an area for future investigation. Our experiments demonstrate that LLMs can "think" via latent-space computations, revealing model-internal inference strategies that need further understanding, especially regarding safety-related concerns such as covert planning, goal-seeking, or deception emerging without explicit token traces.

papers.title: A Theory of Emergent In-Context Learning as Implicit Structure Induction
papers.research_question: When and how does in-context learning (ICL) emerge from generic next-token prediction in language models? The paper investigates the conditions under which ICL capabilities arise from the recombination of compositional operations found in natural language pretraining data.
papers.core_contribution: Provides a theoretical framework showing that in-context learning emerges from next-token prediction when the pretraining distribution has sufficient compositional structure, and validates this with experiments showing ICL emergence in scaled transformer LMs.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning in language models arises from the recombination of compositional structure found in linguistic data, and the paper provides a theoretical and empirical step towards understanding this emergent behavior.
papers.key_findings:
In-context learning emerges when scaling model parameters and data on compositionally structured pretraining distributions.
Prompting models to output intermediate steps (chain-of-thought) provides a theoretical and empirical benefit over direct prompting.
The success of ICL depends on the complexity of the task's compositional description and the iteration complexity of the pretraining data structure.
Probing experiments indicate that in-context learning is supported by the model learning a representation of the input's compositional structure.
The theoretical bounds are independent of the size of the object universe |Ω|, and empirical performance can even improve with larger |Ω|.
papers.limitation: The theoretical analysis considers an idealized predictor with infinite data and capacity, which may not fully capture the complexities of real-world finite transformer models.
future_direction: Exploring more complex compositional structures and their learnability.
Investigating the application of the theory to real-world natural language data and models.
Extending the analysis to longer chains of reasoning and more complex task compositions.
papers.abstract: Scaling large language models (LLMs) leads to an emergent capacity to learn in-context from example demonstrations. Despite progress, theoretical understanding of this phenomenon remains limited. We argue that in-context learning relies on recombination of compositional operations found in natural language data. We derive an information-theoretic bound showing how in-context learning abilities arise from generic next-token prediction when the pretraining distribution has sufficient amounts of compositional structure, under linguistically motivated assumptions. A second bound provides a theoretical justification for the empirical success of prompting LLMs to output intermediate steps towards an answer. To validate theoretical predictions, we introduce a controlled setup for inducing in-context learning; unlike previous approaches, it accounts for the compositional nature of language. Trained transformers can perform in-context learning for a range of tasks, in a manner consistent with the theoretical results. Mirroring real-world LLMs in a miniature setup, in-context learning emerges when scaling parameters and data, and models perform better when prompted to output intermediate steps. Probing shows that in-context learning is supported by a representation of the input's compositional structure. Taken together, these results provide a step towards theoretical understanding of emergent behavior in large language models.

papers.title: On the Biology of a Large Language Model
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally perform computations, and can we reverse engineer their mechanisms using attribution graphs?
papers.core_contribution: This work applies attribution graphs to Claude 3.5 Haiku, uncovering sophisticated internal mechanisms like multi-step reasoning, planning, and metacognitive circuits, demonstrating the value of unsupervised tools for model interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Attribution graphs enable detailed reverse engineering of model internals, revealing complex strategies and advancing the field of AI interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
The model performs genuine two-hop reasoning with intermediate steps, such as representing 'Texas' when answering about the capital of the state containing Dallas.
In poetry generation, the model plans ahead by pre-selecting rhyming words before writing each line.
Multilingual circuits use a mix of language-specific and abstract, language-independent components, with more abstraction in larger models.
Entity recognition circuits distinguish known and unknown entities, influencing when the model answers or refuses, with circuit misfires causing hallucinations.
Refusal mechanisms involve harmful request features aggregated from pretraining and trigger refusal during fine-tuning.
papers.limitation:
tools provide satisfying insight for about a quarter of prompts
replacement model incompletely and imperfectly captures the original model
future_direction: Developing more effective unsupervised exploration tools for increasingly capable models
papers.abstract: How do large language models internally perform computations, and can we reverse engineer their mechanisms using attribution graphs? This work applies attribution graphs to Claude 3.5 Haiku, uncovering sophisticated internal mechanisms like multi-step reasoning, planning, and metacognitive circuits, demonstrating the value of unsupervised tools for model interpretability. Attribution graphs enable detailed reverse engineering of model internals, revealing complex strategies and advancing the field of AI interpretability.

papers.title: Towards Uncovering How Large Language Model Works: An Explainability Perspective
papers.research_question: How can explainability techniques uncover the internal mechanisms of large language models?
papers.core_contribution: This survey paper provides a systematic overview of existing explainability techniques, including mechanistic interpretability and representation engineering, to uncover the inner workings of large language models.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that explainability techniques like mechanistic interpretability and representation engineering are crucial for understanding LLMs, but there are still challenges such as scalability and evaluation of explanations.
papers.limitation: The survey does not explore the complete landscape of relevant XAI methods for understanding LLMs, due to space constraints.
future_direction: Developing scalable techniques to analyze and interpret the intricate knowledge structures embedded within LLMs.
Revealing the intricate mechanisms that give rise to advanced reasoning capabilities in LLMs.
Fully leveraging insights from explainability to develop techniques that can substantially improve LLM performance.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have led to breakthroughs in language tasks, yet the internal mechanisms that enable their remarkable generalization and reasoning abilities remain opaque. This lack of transparency presents challenges such as hallucinations, toxicity, and misalignment with human values, hindering the safe and beneficial deployment of LLMs. This paper aims to uncover the mechanisms underlying LLM functionality through the lens of explainability. First, we review how knowledge is architecturally composed within LLMs and encoded in their internal parameters via mechanistic interpretability techniques. Then, we summarize how knowledge is embedded in LLM representations by leveraging probing techniques and representation engineering. Additionally, we investigate the training dynamics through a mechanistic perspective to explain phenomena such as grokking and memorization. Lastly, we explore how the insights gained from these explanations can enhance LLM performance through model editing, improve efficiency through pruning, and better align with human values.

papers.title: Adaptive Circuit Behavior and Generalization in Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How well does the indirect object identification (IOI) circuit in GPT-2 small generalize to prompt variants that challenge the assumptions of its algorithm?
papers.core_contribution: The IOI circuit generalizes surprisingly well to prompt variants, reusing all its components and mechanisms while only adding additional input edges, and a mechanism called S2 Hacking explains how the circuit outperforms the full model on these variants.
papers.conclusion: The IOI circuit in GPT-2 small generalizes more effectively than previously understood, reusing its core components and mechanisms while adapting through minimal structural changes, offering insights into the broader capabilities of large neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
The base IOI circuit outperforms the full model on DoubleIO and TripleIO prompt variants where the IOI algorithm would fail.
A mechanism termed S2 Hacking explains how the circuit achieves high performance on these variants by focusing on the S2 token due to the knockout procedure.
New circuits discovered for DoubleIO and TripleIO variants reuse all components of the base IOI circuit, only adding edges from additional input tokens (IO2 for DoubleIO, IO2 and IO3 for TripleIO).
The circuit components (attention heads) largely retain their functionalities from the base IOI task when evaluated on the variants.
The order of names in the prompt affects performance, with a 'first come, first serve' mechanism observed in a Previous Token head (2.2).
future_direction: a more detailed study of the duplicate suppression mechanism
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand the inner workings of large neural networks by identifying circuits, or minimal subgraphs within the model that implement algorithms responsible for performing specific tasks. These circuits are typically discovered and analyzed using a narrowly defined prompt format. However, given the abilities of large language models (LLMs) to generalize across various prompt formats for the same task, it remains unclear how well these circuits generalize. For instance, it is unclear whether the models generalization results from reusing the same circuit components, the components behaving differently, or the use of entirely different components. In this paper, we investigate the generality of the indirect object identification (IOI) circuit in GPT-2 small, which is well-studied and believed to implement a simple, interpretable algorithm. We evaluate its performance on prompt variants that challenge the assumptions of this algorithm. Our findings reveal that the circuit generalizes surprisingly well, reusing all of its components and mechanisms while only adding additional input edges. Notably, the circuit generalizes even to prompt variants where the original algorithm should fail; we discover a mechanism that explains this which we term S2 Hacking. Our findings indicate that circuits within LLMs may be more flexible and general than previously recognized, underscoring the importance of studying circuit generalization to better understand the broader capabilities of these models.

papers.title: Emergence of Minimal Circuits for Indirect Object Identification in Attention-Only Transformers
papers.research_question: How do minimal circuits for indirect object identification emerge in attention-only transformers trained from scratch on a symbolic task?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that task-constrained training induces highly interpretable, minimal circuits for indirect object identification in attention-only transformers.
papers.conclusion: Task-constrained training can produce parsimonious and interpretable circuits, offering insight into computational motifs underlying reasoning in larger models.
papers.key_findings:
A single-layer, two-head attention-only transformer achieves perfect accuracy on the symbolic IOI task.
The two heads specialize into additive and contrastive subcircuits that jointly implement IOI resolution.
A two-layer, one-head model achieves similar performance through composition across layers via query-value interactions.
Positional embeddings improve accuracy and interpretability but are not strictly necessary for the task.
The circuits in task-constrained models are more parsimonious than those in broadly pre-trained models.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse-engineer large language models (LLMs) into human-understandable computational circuits. However, the complexity of pretrained models often obscures the minimal mechanisms required for specific reasoning tasks. In this work, we train small, attention-only transformers from scratch on a symbolic version of the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) task -- a benchmark for studying coreference -- like reasoning in transformers. Surprisingly, a single-layer model with only two attention heads achieves perfect IOI accuracy, despite lacking MLPs and normalization layers. Through residual stream decomposition, spectral analysis, and embedding interventions, we find that the two heads specialize into additive and contrastive subcircuits that jointly implement IOI resolution. Furthermore, we show that a two-layer, one-head model achieves similar performance by composing information across layers through query-value interactions. These results demonstrate that task-specific training induces highly interpretable, minimal circuits, offering a controlled testbed for probing the computational foundations of transformer reasoning.

papers.title: How Interpretable are Reasoning Explanations from Prompting Large Language Models?
papers.research_question: How interpretable are reasoning explanations from prompting large language models? The paper investigates this by evaluating the faithfulness, robustness, and utility of explanations generated by various prompting techniques.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces SEA-CoT, a prompting technique designed to improve the interpretability (faithfulness, robustness, utility) of reasoning explanations from LLMs, and provides a comprehensive evaluation framework for interpretability across multiple prompting methods and benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: The proposed SEA-CoT framework improves the interpretability of reasoning explanations across multiple dimensions, and the work provides a multifaceted evaluation methodology for assessing explanation quality in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
SEA-CoT outperforms other prompting techniques (CoT, SC-CoT, QD, Self-Refine) in aggregate interpretability scores across faithfulness, robustness, and utility on commonsense reasoning benchmarks.
A single LLM setup for generating explanations and answers yields higher faithfulness and utility than a modular approach with separate explainer and predictor models.
Larger model sizes (e.g., Llama-2 70B) generally produce more interpretable explanations than smaller sizes, but SEA-CoT enables smaller models (7B) to outperform larger models using other prompts.
The selection of reasoning chains based on both entailment and keyword overlap (SEA-CoT) is more effective for interpretability than selection based on maximum probability or random choice.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to a single LLM family (Llama-2) and does not explore other architectures or larger models like GPT-3.5/4.
The quality of automatic modifications (paraphrasing, mistake insertion, counterfactual generation) depends on the capability of the modifier models (GPT-3.5/GPT-4).
The work does not investigate techniques that ground LLM responses with external knowledge.
The work does not address the issue of self-hallucination in LLMs.
The work does not explore hybrid approaches like neuro-symbolic AI.
future_direction: Extend the investigation to transformers of different structures (encoder or encoder-decoder) and larger models like GPT-3.5/4.
Improve the quality of automatic modifications to explanations.
Incorporate external knowledge grounding into the interpretability framework.
Investigate hybrid approaches such as neuro-symbolic AI.
papers.abstract: Prompt Engineering has garnered significant attention for enhancing the performance of large language models across a multitude of tasks. Techniques such as the Chain-of-Thought not only bolster task performance but also delineate a clear trajectory of reasoning steps, offering a tangible form of explanation for the audience. Prior works on interpretability assess the reasoning chains yielded by Chain-of-Thought solely along a singular axis, namely faithfulness. We present a comprehensive and multifaceted evaluation of interpretability, examining not only faithfulness but also robustness and utility across multiple commonsense reasoning benchmarks. Likewise, our investigation is not confined to a single prompting technique; it expansively covers a multitude of prevalent prompting techniques employed in large language models, thereby ensuring a wide-ranging and exhaustive evaluation. In addition, we introduce a simple interpretability alignment technique, termed Self-Entailment-Alignment Chain-of-thought, that yields more than 70\% improvements across multiple dimensions of interpretability. Code is available at https://github.com/SenticNet/CoT_interpretability

papers.title: ShortGPT: Layers in Large Language Models are More Redundant Than You Expect
papers.research_question: How redundant are the layers in large language models, and can a simple layer removal method based on a new importance metric effectively prune them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies significant layer redundancy in LLMs and introduces Block Influence (BI) to measure layer importance. Based on BI, the proposed ShortGPT method removes redundant layers, achieving competitive pruning results without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit significant layer-wise redundancy, and a simple pruning method based on layer removal (ShortGPT) can effectively compress models with minimal performance loss, offering insights for future model compression and training efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Layers in LLMs are redundant, especially in the middle to later layers, and removing them individually causes minimal performance degradation.
The proposed Block Influence (BI) metric, based on cosine similarity between a layer's input and output hidden states, correlates with layer importance.
ShortGPT, a simple layer removal method based on BI, outperforms previous state-of-the-art pruning methods and maintains ~90% performance while reducing ~25% parameters.
The redundancy phenomenon is not unique to transformers; it also exists in non-transformer models like Mamba and RWKV.
ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization and can be combined with it for further compression.
papers.limitation: Layer removal has a more significant negative effect on generative tasks compared to multiple-choice tasks, especially for smaller models.
future_direction: Exploring post-training to restore performance after pruning
Improving model training efficiency by reducing inherent redundancy
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance in performance, their size has escalated significantly, with current LLMs containing billions or even trillions of parameters. However, in this study, we discovered that many layers of LLMs exhibit high similarity, and some layers play a negligible role in network functionality. Based on this observation, we define a metric called Block Influence (BI) to gauge the significance of each layer in LLMs. We then propose a straightforward pruning approach: layer removal, in which we directly delete the redundant layers in LLMs based on their BI scores. Experiments demonstrate that our method, which we call ShortGPT, significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in model pruning. Moreover, ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization-like methods, enabling further reduction in parameters and computation. The ability to achieve better results through simple layer removal, as opposed to more complex pruning techniques, suggests a high degree of redundancy in the model architecture.

papers.title: On Memorization of Large Language Models in Logical Reasoning
papers.research_question: Does memorization explain LLMs' performance on reasoning benchmarks, and is memorization only detrimental to learning to reason?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a memorization score (LiMem) and a dynamic K&K benchmark to show that fine-tuned LLMs memorize training puzzles but also improve in generalization, developing reasoning skills alongside memorization.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that memorization and reasoning coexist in fine-tuned LLMs, and the proposed memorization score (LiMem) helps quantify the interplay between them.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can interpolate and memorize training puzzles after fine-tuning, achieving near-perfect accuracy, but struggle with slight variations.
Fine-tuning leads to heavy memorization but also consistently improves generalization performance on K&K puzzles.
LLMs develop reasoning skills on K&K puzzles alongside memorization, as shown by transferability across difficulty levels and probing internal representations.
Fine-tuning with detailed reasoning steps (CoT) can further boost generalization, even when fine-tuned with wrong reasoning steps.
Per-sample memorization score reveals how LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization when solving logical puzzles.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to Knights and Knaves puzzles and may not generalize to other reasoning tasks.
The memorization score LiMem may not capture all forms of memorization.
future_direction: Extend the study to other reasoning tasks beyond K&K puzzles.
Investigate the effect of model scale on memorization and reasoning.
Improve the memorization score to better capture memorization behaviors.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve good performance on challenging reasoning benchmarks, yet could also make basic reasoning mistakes. This contrasting behavior is puzzling when it comes to understanding the mechanisms behind LLMs' reasoning capabilities. One hypothesis is that the increasingly high and nearly saturated performance on common reasoning benchmarks could be due to the memorization of similar problems. In this paper, we systematically investigate this hypothesis with a quantitative measurement of memorization in reasoning tasks, using a dynamically generated logical reasoning benchmark based on Knights and Knaves (K&K) puzzles. We found that LLMs could interpolate the training puzzles (achieving near-perfect accuracy) after fine-tuning, yet fail when those puzzles are slightly perturbed, suggesting that the models heavily rely on memorization to solve those training puzzles. On the other hand, we show that while fine-tuning leads to heavy memorization, it also consistently improves generalization performance. In-depth analyses with perturbation tests, cross difficulty-level transferability, probing model internals, and fine-tuning with wrong answers suggest that the LLMs learn to reason on K&K puzzles despite training data memorization. This phenomenon indicates that LLMs exhibit a complex interplay between memorization and genuine reasoning abilities. Finally, our analysis with per-sample memorization score sheds light on how LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization in solving logical puzzles. Our code and data are available at https://memkklogic.github.io.

papers.title: A Practical Review of Mechanistic Interpretability for Transformer-Based Language Models
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a comprehensive survey of mechanistic interpretability (MI) for transformer-based language models, organizing the field from a task-centric perspective and presenting a beginner's roadmap to guide newcomers.
papers.conclusion: The survey synthesizes the current state of mechanistic interpretability for transformer-based LMs, highlights existing challenges, and outlines promising future research directions to advance the field.
papers.key_findings:
Mechanistic interpretability research can be organized around three fundamental objects of study: features, circuits, and universality.
The field has developed a variety of techniques, including vocabulary projection, intervention-based methods, and sparse autoencoders, each with distinct advantages and limitations.
MI has yielded insights into model capabilities such as in-context learning, reasoning, and knowledge mechanisms, and has applications in model enhancement and AI safety.
Current challenges include the scalability of techniques, the need for standardized benchmarks, and the practical utility of MI findings.
Future directions include advancing MI techniques, improving automated hypothesis generation, and exploring new paradigms of human-AI collaboration.
future_direction: Advancement in MI techniques to improve scalability and generalizability.
Development of standardized benchmarks and metrics for evaluating interpretability methods.
Exploration of automated hypothesis generation and new paradigms of human-AI collaboration driven by MI.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability (MI) is an emerging sub-field of interpretability that seeks to understand a neural network model by reverse-engineering its internal computations. Recently, MI has garnered significant attention for interpreting transformer-based language models (LMs), resulting in many novel insights yet introducing new challenges. However, there has not been work that comprehensively reviews these insights and challenges, particularly as a guide for newcomers to this field. To fill this gap, we provide a comprehensive survey from a task-centric perspective, organizing the taxonomy of MI research around specific research questions or tasks. We outline the fundamental objects of study in MI, along with the techniques, evaluation methods, and key findings for each task in the taxonomy. In particular, we present a task-centric taxonomy as a roadmap for beginners to navigate the field by helping them quickly identify impactful problems in which they are most interested and leverage MI for their benefit. Finally, we discuss the current gaps in the field and suggest potential future directions for MI research.

papers.title: Internalizing LLM Reasoning via Discovery and Replay of Latent Actions
papers.research_question: How can we dynamically control latent trajectories to internalize reasoning processes in LLMs, improving accuracy and efficiency?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes STIR, a framework that internalizes reasoning by distilling latent steering tools from model rollouts and dynamically controlling trajectories, improving accuracy and efficiency.
papers.conclusion: STIR bridges the gap between static activation steering and dynamic reasoning, enabling efficient high-fidelity cognitive modeling by internalizing explicit reasoning into latent dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
STIR improves average reasoning accuracy by 1.9% to 7.5% compared to standard chain-of-thought decoding.
STIR reduces average token consumption by up to 35%.
STIR establishes a new accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier.
The framework captures transferable latent tools that generalize across tasks.
Dynamic control adapts to non-stationary reasoning processes better than static steering.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on extracting steering impulses at predefined structural delimiters, which may restrict granularity of control.
Corrective efficacy bounded by geometric diversity of failure modes captured during offline discovery.
Effectiveness of anchor gating depends on precision of latent similarity metrics in high-dimensional spaces.
Evaluation primarily targets verification-friendly reasoning tasks, extending to open-ended domains is challenging.
papers.abstract: The internalization of chain-of-thought processes into hidden states has emerged as a highly efficient paradigm for scaling test-time compute. However, existing activation steering methods rely on static control vectors that fail to adapt to the non-stationary evolution of complex reasoning tasks. To address this limitation, we propose STIR (Self-Distilled Tools for Internal Reasoning), a framework that reformulates reasoning enhancement as a dynamic latent trajectory control problem. STIR introduces a synergistic three-stage pipeline: (1) differential intrinsic action induction harvests latent reasoning successes to crystallize steering primitives; (2) sparse control basis construction curates a compact, geometrically diverse tool library; and (3) value-modulated trajectory intervention dynamically injects context-specific impulses via anchor-based gating. Extensive experiments on six arithmetic and logical benchmarks across four representative models demonstrate that STIR improves average accuracy by 1.9% to 7.5% while reducing average token consumption by up to 35% compared to vanilla decoding. These findings demonstrate that the benefits of explicit chain-of-thought can be realized through dynamic latent trajectory control, internalizing the reasoning process to bypass the explicit generation while achieving superior fidelity. Our code is available at https://github.com/sznnzs/LLM-Latent-Action.

papers.title: What needs to go right for an induction head? A mechanistic study of in-context learning circuits and their formation
papers.research_question: Why is there more than one induction head, and how are they dependent on each other? Why do induction heads appear all of a sudden, and what are the subcircuits that enable them to emerge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an artificial optogenetics framework for causal manipulation of activations during training and uses it to identify three interacting subcircuits that explain the phase change in induction head formation.
papers.conclusion: The study provides a deeper understanding of induction head formation and phase changes through the identification of subcircuits, and the introduced framework enables causal analysis of training dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Multiple induction heads form and contribute additively to minimize loss.
Induction heads and previous token heads are wired in a many-to-many fashion.
Three underlying subcircuits (match, copy, and routing) interact to drive the phase change in induction head formation.
The timing of the phase change depends on data properties, which can be understood through the subcircuits.
The network uses additional capacity (multiple heads) for faster training even when not strictly necessary.
papers.abstract: In-context learning is a powerful emergent ability in transformer models.
